trig-polar-parametric-polar-coordinate-s.title: Polar coordinate system
trig-polar-parametric-polar-coordinate-s.summary: Use distance and a directed angle to locate points, including negative radii and multiple representations of the same position.

blocks.text: A polar coordinate pair (r,θ) identifies a point r units along a ray making angle θ with the positive x-axis. The angle is measured counterclockwise when positive. A negative radius reverses the ray direction by π radians. The origin is represented by (0,θ) for any θ, so polar coordinates are not unique.

blocks.caption: Original polar-coordinate grid showing negative radius and angle equivalence; use formulas for exact values.

blocks.title: Locate (3, 5π/6)
blocks.strategy: Convert the polar representation into its Cartesian coordinates to confirm the quadrant.
steps: Therefore x=−3√3/2 and y=3/2; the point lies in Quadrant II.
blocks.check: Both the x sign and y sign match Quadrant II.

blocks.title: Find a positive-radius equivalent of (−2, π/3)
blocks.problem: Find a positive-radius equivalent of (−2, π/3)
blocks.strategy: Reverse the negative radius and rotate the angle by π.
steps: The equivalent positive-radius pair is (2,4π/3).
blocks.check: Check directly: both representations have x=−1 and y=−√3.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: The radius is not automatically positive. Do not confuse (−r,θ) with (r,θ); a negative r flips the point to the opposite ray.

blocks.explanation: Negating the radius moves four units left; using positive r requires θ=π.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Lial 10th ed. §8.5; Sullivan 9th ed. §5.1; Kelley Ch. 17. Interpret angle intervals and plotted diagrams using the stated mathematical conventions.

trig-polar-parametric-rectangular-and-po.title: Rectangular and polar conversion
trig-polar-parametric-rectangular-and-po.summary: Convert points and equations between rectangular (x,y) and polar (r,θ), choosing a quadrant-correct argument and preserving special cases.

blocks.text: For a polar point, x=r cosθ and y=r sinθ. The squared-radius equation r²=x²+y² avoids sign ambiguity. For a non-origin rectangular point, take r=√(x²+y²)≥0 and choose θ using the correct quadrant (atan2 is convenient). Equation conversions must account for r=0 before dividing by r.

blocks.caption: Original polar-coordinate grid showing negative radius and angle equivalence; use formulas for exact values.

blocks.title: Convert (−3,3√3) to polar coordinates
blocks.strategy: Compute a nonnegative radius, then choose θ in Quadrant II.
steps: The reference angle is π/3 and the point is in Quadrant II; θ=2π/3, giving (6,2π/3).

blocks.title: Convert the circle x²+y²=4x into polar form
blocks.problem: Convert the circle x²+y²=4x into polar form
blocks.strategy: Substitute r² for x²+y² and r cosθ for x; retain the origin.
steps: Substituting yields r²=4r cosθ.
Keep r(r−4cosθ)=0 as the full relation; r=4cosθ is also a complete locus here because the origin occurs when cosθ=0.
blocks.check: The rectangular circle is centered at (2,0) with radius 2, and passes through the origin.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Using arctan(y/x) alone can lose the quadrant. Dividing a polar equation by r may silently remove origin solutions.

blocks.prompt: Find polar coordinates with r≥0 for (0,−5).
blocks.explanation: The point lies on the negative y-axis, five units from the origin.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Lial 10th ed. §§8.2, 8.5; Sullivan 9th ed. §5.1; Kelley Ch. 17. Interpret angle intervals and plotted diagrams using the stated mathematical conventions.

trig-polar-parametric-polar-graphing-and.title: Polar graphing and symmetry
trig-polar-parametric-polar-graphing-and.summary: Trace polar graphs by sampling angles, finding zeros and maxima, and testing symmetry using equivalence of polar pairs rather than unreliable shortcuts.

blocks.text: A polar equation r=f(θ) describes a locus as θ varies. Construct a small value table, use Cartesian coordinates for key points, and check repetitions. Negative r plots in the opposite direction. Standard polar-symmetry substitution tests are sufficient when an equation is unchanged, but a failed algebraic test does not prove geometric asymmetry.

blocks.caption: Original polar-coordinate grid showing negative radius and angle equivalence; use formulas for exact values.

blocks.title: Trace r=2cosθ at key angles
blocks.strategy: Sample θ=0,π/2,π to understand the circle geometry.
steps: At θ=0: r=2 gives (2,0); at θ=π/2: r=0 gives the origin.
At θ=π: r=−2, which also maps to (2,0). Converting gives x²+y²=2x.
blocks.check: The graph is a circle of radius 1 centered at (1,0).

blocks.title: Test symmetry of r=1+cosθ about the polar axis
blocks.problem: Test symmetry of r=1+cosθ about the polar axis
steps: Because cos(−θ)=cosθ, r(−θ)=1+cosθ=r(θ).
Matching points occur reflected across the x-axis; hence the curve is polar-axis symmetric.
blocks.check: The graph has a rightward bulge and a cusp at the pole when θ=π.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Do not treat a negative r value as a missing point. A symmetry substitution that does not reproduce the equation may be inconclusive.

blocks.prompt: Where does r=1+cosθ meet the pole?
blocks.explanation: Set r=0 and solve cosθ=−1; this occurs only when θ=π+2πk.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Lial 10th ed. §8.5; Sullivan 9th ed. §5.2; Kelley Ch. 17. Interpret angle intervals and plotted diagrams using the stated mathematical conventions.

trig-polar-parametric-common-polar-curve.title: Common polar curves
trig-polar-parametric-common-polar-curve.summary: Recognize polar lines, circles, cardioids, limaçons, rose curves, and lemniscates using their equations, symmetries, zeros, and tracing intervals.

blocks.text: Polar families produce shapes that are difficult to see in rectangular form. Examples include r=a cosθ (a circle through the pole), r=a±b cosθ (limaçons, with a cardioid when |a|=|b|≠0), r=a cos(nθ) or a sin(nθ) (rose curves), and r²=a²cos2θ (lemniscate where the right-hand side is nonnegative).

blocks.caption: Original polar-coordinate grid showing negative radius and angle equivalence; use formulas for exact values.

blocks.title: Identify r=4sin(3θ)
blocks.strategy: Recognize the rose equation and use n to count petals.
steps: This is r=a sin(nθ) with a=4, n=3.
Since n is odd, there are three petals, each with maximum radius 4.
blocks.check: The three maxima occur at angles solving sin(3θ)=1, spaced by 2π/3.

blocks.title: Identify r=2+2cosθ
blocks.strategy: Compare the coefficients of the constant and cosine terms.
steps: It has form r=a+bcosθ with a=b=2.
It is a cardioid; it meets the pole at θ=π and reaches r=4 at θ=0.
blocks.check: The cardioid points to the right and is symmetric about the polar axis.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Do not apply the rose-petal rule to noninteger n. For r²=a²cos2θ, only angles giving r²≥0 are allowed.

blocks.prompt: How many petals does r=3cos(4θ) have?
blocks.explanation: With even positive integer n=4, a rose has 2n=8 petals.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Sullivan 9th ed. §5.2; Lial 10th ed. §8.5; Kelley Ch. 17. Interpret angle intervals and plotted diagrams using the stated mathematical conventions.

trig-polar-parametric-parametric-equatio.title: Parametric equations
trig-polar-parametric-parametric-equatio.summary: Represent planar paths with x(t), y(t), understand their direction and parameter intervals, and eliminate a parameter without losing restrictions.

blocks.text: Parametric equations specify coordinates as functions of a parameter t: (x(t),y(t)). The parameter interval and the order of traversal are part of the description. Different parametrizations may trace the same locus in opposite directions or multiple times. Eliminating t gives the Cartesian locus but can lose orientation and parameter-range information.

blocks.caption: Original parametric circle diagram showing increasing parameter and direction of travel; not drawn to scale for exact values.

blocks.title: Eliminate t from x=2t+1, y=t²
blocks.strategy: Solve the first equation and substitute into the second.
steps: Therefore y=(x−1)²/4; if t≥0, only x≥1 is traced.
blocks.check: Check t=0: the path starts at (1,0) and moves toward increasing x.

blocks.title: Trace x=3cos t, y=3sin t, 0≤t≤π
blocks.strategy: Use the circle identity and evaluate the endpoints and midpoint.
steps: x²+y²=9 is the Cartesian circle.
t=0 gives (3,0), t=π/2 gives (0,3), t=π gives (−3,0).
blocks.check: Only the upper semicircle is traced, counterclockwise from right to left.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Do not label the entire Cartesian curve as the traced path when t is restricted. Eliminating t also hides direction and possible repeated traversal.

blocks.prompt: For x=t, y=t², 0≤t≤2, which part is traced?
blocks.explanation: Since x=t, the parameter interval directly restricts x and fixes the traversal direction.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Lial 10th ed. §8.6; Sullivan 9th ed. §6.7; Kelley Ch. 17. Interpret angle intervals and plotted diagrams using the stated mathematical conventions.

trig-polar-parametric-conversion-and-gra.title: Conversion and graphical interpretation
trig-polar-parametric-conversion-and-gra.summary: Relate polar and parametric representations, interpret a curve’s direction and repeats, and preserve all restrictions when converting to a rectangular equation.

blocks.text: A polar graph r=f(θ) has natural parametrization x(θ)=f(θ)cosθ, y(θ)=f(θ)sinθ. Conversely, for a parametric path use r(t)=√(x(t)²+y(t)²) and θ(t)=atan2(y(t),x(t)) away from the origin. An eliminated Cartesian equation describes the locus but not necessarily the orientation, number of traversals, or exact endpoints.

blocks.caption: Original parametric circle diagram showing increasing parameter and direction of travel; not drawn to scale for exact values.

blocks.title: Parametrize r=2sinθ for 0≤θ≤π
blocks.strategy: Treat θ as the parameter and convert pointwise.
steps: x(θ)=2sinθcosθ=sin2θ.
y(θ)=2sin²θ=1−cos2θ, and x²+(y−1)²=1.
blocks.check: The circle centered at (0,1) is traced once over 0≤θ≤π; its start and end are the pole.

blocks.title: Interpret x=cos(2t), y=sin(2t), 0≤t≤2π
blocks.strategy: Convert to the circle equation and track the angle.
steps: The locus is x²+y²=1.
The position angle is 2t, which increases from 0 to 4π, so the path is traced twice counterclockwise.
blocks.check: At t=0,π,2π the point is (1,0), showing repeat traversal.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Converting to x²+y²=constant discards how many times a path is traced. At the origin, the angle θ is not uniquely determined.

blocks.prompt: How many laps does x=cos3t, y=sin3t make for 0≤t≤2π?
blocks.explanation: The angle 3t runs from 0 through 6π, which comprises three complete positive rotations.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original explanations and exercises): Lial 10th ed. §§8.5–8.6; Sullivan 9th ed. §§5.1–5.2, 6.7; Kelley Ch. 17. Interpret angle intervals and plotted diagrams using the stated mathematical conventions.
